narrative: The model estimates a 46% chance that you will leave your job. That does not mean departure is certain, but in this promotion decision it was treated as a meaningful retention risk, so you were denied the promotion. The strongest influence was your total work experience. You have one to five years overall, which is common among employees predicted to stay, so this factor actually worked in your favor and lowered the estimated risk. The next most important factor was whether you have other job opportunities. You do have other opportunities, while most employees predicted to stay do not, so this pushed the estimate toward leaving. The third factor was your sector. You work in the “other” sector, which is somewhat less common among stayers than medical or education, so it added a smaller push toward leaving. Although your experience suggested stability, these opportunity and sector signals outweighed it enough to create a notable leave risk. Other profile details, such as low job support, no recognition, psychological exhaustion, no bonus, and no medical insurance, may also have contributed. Rather than treating this as a final judgment, the organization should discuss your career path, recognition, support, and retention incentives. You may also want to clarify what would make you stay, such as promotion criteria, training, and rewards.
